title: What is a REIT? Follow the asset, the income and the claim
description: Understand how a US REIT earns income, what shareholders own, and why a dividend is different from a guaranteed property return.

sections.heading: A structure, not a single business
sections.text: A real estate investment trust is a company that owns, operates or finances income-producing real estate. In the United States, REIT tax treatment comes with tests covering assets, income, ownership and distributions. The label does not tell you whether the company collects apartment rent, leases warehouses or holds mortgage securities. Begin by identifying the actual business. An equity REIT generally owns properties; a mortgage REIT generally supplies real-estate financing. Their cash-flow drivers and useful analytical measures differ.

sections.heading: What a shareholder actually owns
sections.text: Buying a listed REIT share gives you an equity claim on the company, not title to a particular apartment or a right to a particular tenant's rent. Property expenses, interest, corporate overhead, reinvestment and other claims come before cash available to common shareholders. A stock exchange makes shares tradable during market hours, but the quoted price can be far below an estimate of underlying property value. Liquidity is the ability to transact, not protection against a loss.

sections.heading: Why the distribution rule does not insure the dividend
sections.text: The familiar US requirement generally concerns distributing at least 90% of REIT taxable income, excluding net capital gains, subject to applicable rules. Taxable income is not rent, revenue, GAAP net income, FFO or AFFO. Management may distribute more than the minimum, and a historical dividend may become unaffordable. Accounting depreciation is one reason taxable income and operating measures can differ. A dividend payment is therefore evidence of a payment, not proof that recurring operations funded it.

sections.heading: Two reasonable ways to look at the same REIT
sections.text: An income-focused reader may value recurring rent and regular distributions. A balance-sheet-focused reader may worry about refinancing, tenant concentration or the equity needed to fund growth. Both can be right. Long leases may stabilize current revenue while delaying the ability to raise rents. A useful first review pairs the business description with the debt note and cash-flow statement. Then examine the issuer's reconciliation of its chosen performance measures, rather than comparing a headline yield in isolation.

example.heading: Hypothetical: rent is not the dividend
example.text: Suppose properties collect $100 of rent, incur $30 of operating costs, and the company pays $15 of interest and overhead. That leaves $55 before capital spending and other items. If recurring improvements require $10, the simplified remaining amount is $45. A $50 distribution would require another funding source in this example. This cash illustration is neither a tax calculation nor a complete FFO reconciliation.

pitfall: A 7% quoted yield does not mean that rent, earnings or your investment value will grow 7%. Price losses and dividend reductions can outweigh income.
checklist: Identify equity ownership versus mortgage financing.
Read the property mix and largest tenant exposures.
Compare the dividend with a reconciled, appropriate operating measure.
Inspect recurring capital needs and debt due over the next few years.

title: Listed, non-traded and private REITs: access changes the risk
description: Separate a REIT's business model from its trading structure, liquidity, fees and disclosure obligations.

sections.heading: Use two separate classification questions
sections.text: First ask what the REIT does: own real estate, finance it, or combine activities. Then ask how the investment is offered and traded. A listed equity REIT and a non-traded equity REIT can own similar buildings but give investors very different liquidity and price-discovery experiences. Publicly traded, public non-listed and private are distribution and market-access categories. Apartment, industrial and office are property categories. Mixing these axes hides important risks.

sections.heading: Listed shares make price changes visible
sections.text: Listed REITs trade on an exchange and file public disclosures. Prices respond to interest rates, expected rent growth, financing conditions and investor sentiment. Daily volatility can be uncomfortable, but it also provides an observable price at which other investors are willing to trade. That price is not an appraisal and does not necessarily equal the company's net asset value. Bid-ask spreads, market conditions and order size can affect the actual execution price.

sections.heading: Non-traded does not mean low-risk
sections.text: Public non-listed REITs have public reporting obligations but their shares do not trade on a national securities exchange. Repurchase programs may have limits, gates, discounts or suspension provisions. Private REITs can have more restricted access and less public information. Infrequently updated values may look smoother than listed share prices while underlying properties still face the same vacancies, repair bills and debt maturities. Read redemption terms instead of assuming an exit will be available.

sections.heading: Compare the net experience, not just advertised income
sections.text: One investor may prioritize exchange liquidity; another may accept illiquidity for a particular strategy. The useful comparison includes all fees, leverage, valuation procedures, distribution funding and the realistic holding period. A distribution funded in part from offering proceeds or borrowing does not carry the same implication as recurring operating income. For every vehicle, read the prospectus or offering documents and financial statements. Understand whether the quoted distribution rate reflects a purchase price, an estimated NAV or another denominator.

example.heading: Hypothetical: a redemption limit
example.text: An investor holds $20,000 in a vehicle and requests a full redemption. If only $4,000 of that request is accepted under the program's terms, the investor still has $16,000 invested and exposed to subsequent valuation changes. This is a liquidity illustration, not a description of a specific REIT's repurchase policy.

pitfall: A stable published NAV or a regular distribution is not evidence that an investment can be sold quickly at that value.
checklist: Locate the actual repurchase and suspension provisions.
Distinguish upfront, recurring and performance-related fees.
Read how distributions were funded.
Check the age and methodology of the reported valuation.

title: The 90% REIT rule: taxable income is not cash flow
description: Why the US distribution requirement cannot be used as a dividend safety test or an AFFO payout target.

sections.heading: Keep the tax base attached to the percentage
sections.text: The commonly cited US REIT distribution requirement generally means at least 90% of REIT taxable income, excluding net capital gains and subject to applicable adjustments. Removing the phrase taxable income changes the meaning. It does not require a company to pay out 90% of rent collected, property value, operating cash flow or AFFO. Tax rules also address qualification, timing and other matters; the percentage alone is not a complete guide to REIT taxation.

sections.heading: Why several income numbers coexist
sections.text: GAAP net income follows financial reporting rules. Taxable income follows tax rules. FFO adjusts selected real-estate accounting items, and AFFO is an issuer-defined non-GAAP measure. Depreciation and transaction treatment can make these amounts diverge. A company can distribute a large fraction of taxable income while retaining a larger fraction of its reported AFFO. That does not eliminate its capital spending, debt repayments or other uses of cash.

sections.heading: Qualification and sustainability answer different questions
sections.text: A qualification calculation asks whether a legal distribution requirement has been satisfied. A sustainability review asks how future dividends will be funded through a range of operating and financing conditions. Property maintenance, lease incentives, maturities and preferred dividends all matter. Funding a distribution with asset sales may be sensible during a portfolio transition, yet it cannot be assumed to repeat indefinitely. Examine cash sources over several years rather than treating one year's distribution as a permanent run rate.

sections.heading: The shareholder tax result is another separate question
sections.text: The tax character of a distribution can differ from the issuer's operating narrative. Ordinary income, capital-gain distributions and return-of-capital components may have different treatments depending on jurisdiction, account type and the investor's circumstances. Do not use an AFFO payout ratio to determine your tax bill. Use the issuer's final tax reporting and the relevant tax authority's guidance. The site's calculators use an explicit user-supplied withholding assumption, not a determination of tax liability.

example.heading: Hypothetical: two denominators
example.text: Assume REIT taxable income is $60 and an issuer reports $100 of AFFO for the same period. A simplified 90% calculation gives $54, while a $75 common distribution would be a 75% AFFO payout. These are different calculations. The example omits qualification adjustments, capital gains and timing rules and does not establish any company's required distribution.

pitfall: Neither a 90% distribution requirement nor a payout below 90% of AFFO establishes that the current dividend is safe.
checklist: Name the income measure and period for every percentage.
Read the issuer's distribution and tax disclosures.
Separate recurring funding from sales, borrowing and new equity.
Use final tax documents for personal reporting.

title: How to read a REIT filing without getting lost
description: A practical reading sequence for the 10-K, 10-Q, earnings release and supplemental operating tables.

sections.heading: Start with a question and the right period
sections.text: A filing is easier to read when you have a question: did recurring income per share improve, are leases rolling at higher rents, or is a maturity becoming expensive? Start with the latest annual 10-K for the business and audited statements, then the subsequent 10-Qs for changes. Earnings releases and supplements can add property-level detail and non-GAAP reconciliations. Check publication dates and reporting periods. A quarter, a year-to-date amount and full-year guidance are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: Read the business before the ratios
sections.text: The business section explains what the company owns and how it earns money. Risk factors identify exposures, although not every risk has equal probability. Management's discussion and analysis explains movements in results and liquidity. Read geographic, tenant and property concentrations alongside the operating tables. A tenant's percentage of annualized rent is not necessarily its percentage of cash collected, and a headline occupancy rate may exclude properties under development.

sections.heading: Tie the release back to the statements
sections.text: Follow the reconciliation from net income to FFO and any adjusted metric. Mark each adjustment as recurring, non-recurring, cash or non-cash where the evidence supports that classification. Then read the cash-flow statement and notes on debt, leases, acquisitions and joint ventures. A favorable adjusted number can coexist with substantial financing needs. Record both the issuer's explanation and any unresolved reconciliation differences instead of filling gaps with assumptions.

sections.heading: Keep a reproducible evidence trail
sections.text: Save the document title, filing date, page or table, units and the exact measure used. Note whether figures are consolidated or proportionate, common-share or total-company, and basic or diluted per share. A sensible counterargument to a pessimistic balance-sheet view may be available liquidity or contractual rent growth. A counterargument to optimistic earnings guidance may be capex excluded from the measure. The objective is to make both readings testable from documents, not to select only supportive facts.

example.heading: Hypothetical: annualizing a quarter
example.text: An earnings release reports $0.80 of quarterly FFO per diluted share. Multiplying by four gives a $3.20 annualized illustration, not full-year guidance. A disposition in the next quarter or seasonal hotel results can make that shortcut misleading. Label the period, and use actual trailing figures or management guidance separately.

pitfall: An earnings presentation is a useful map, but its selected charts are not a substitute for the financial statements and notes.
checklist: Record the document date, period, units and table location.
Read non-GAAP definitions and reconciliations.
Check debt and joint-venture notes.
Write down what remains unknown and the next disclosure that could resolve it.

title: Dividend yield versus total return: count both sides
description: Calculate income and price change together, and understand why a rising dividend yield can be a warning rather than a reward.

sections.heading: Yield describes a ratio at a price
sections.text: Dividend yield divides an annual dividend amount by a share price. The numerator might be the most recent payment annualized, trailing twelve-month payments, or an analyst forecast. Those conventions can produce different yields for the same security. A special distribution can distort the trailing figure. Always identify the basis. Yield tells you how an assumed distribution compares with price; it does not tell you whether that distribution will continue.

sections.heading: Total return includes the changing claim
sections.text: For one share held over a period, a simple total return includes the ending price minus the starting price plus cash distributions, divided by the starting price. It ignores reinvestment timing, transaction costs and taxes unless explicitly adjusted. A high cash yield can coexist with a negative total return when the share price falls. Conversely, a lower-yielding business may generate stronger total return if per-share cash generation and market value rise.

sections.heading: Yield on cost answers a narrower question
sections.text: Yield on cost compares today's annual dividend with your historical purchase price. It can help describe income growth on an original investment, but it is not the yield available to a new investor or the opportunity cost of keeping the position. Decisions made today involve today's market value. A long-held position with a high yield on cost can still face deteriorating coverage, expensive refinancing or concentration risk.

sections.heading: Compare scenarios rather than chasing the largest number
sections.text: An income-oriented investor may prefer regular cash distributions, while another values reinvestment inside the business. Neither preference makes a headline yield a safety score. Model an unchanged dividend, a reduction and a price change separately. Reinvesting dividends buys more shares but does not erase the risk of a falling asset value. If you compare a REIT with a bond, remember that the common equity dividend and redemption value are not contractual bond payments.

example.heading: Hypothetical: 6% income, negative return
example.text: Buy one share for $100, receive $6 in distributions and finish the year with a share worth $90. Simple pretax total return is ($90 − $100 + $6) ÷ $100 = −4%. The initial 6% yield was an income ratio, not a promise of a positive return. Reinvestment, taxes and fees would change the realized result.

pitfall: A falling share price mechanically increases the indicated yield if the assumed dividend stays unchanged. It may be signaling risk that the current dividend does not yet reflect.
checklist: Specify trailing, indicated or forecast dividends.
Separate recurring distributions from special payments.
Show price change alongside cash income.
Use consistent currencies and account for fees and tax assumptions.

title: Dividend reinvestment: compounding with assumptions visible
description: Understand what a DRIP changes, what it cannot fix, and how to interpret a constant-yield reinvestment model.

sections.heading: Reinvestment changes the number of shares
sections.text: A dividend reinvestment plan uses distributions to purchase additional shares under the plan's terms. If a payment is reinvested at a lower price, it can buy more shares; at a higher price, fewer. Fractional-share handling, fees and the execution date depend on the broker or issuer. The key distinction is that receiving cash and reinvesting cash are two steps. A dividend is not an extra return that can be added on top of a total-return figure already including distributions.

sections.heading: A smooth model is a controlled experiment
sections.text: The calculator on this site applies a constant annual distribution yield to the modeled balance in monthly periods, with optional monthly contributions and a user-set withholding assumption. That makes the compounding arithmetic inspectable. Real prices, dividend rates, tax treatment and payment schedules vary. A constant-yield model does not predict a particular REIT's share count or future market price. Use it to understand the effect of time, contributions and reinvestment, then stress the inputs.

sections.heading: Tax and concentration do not disappear
sections.text: Reinvestment may still involve taxable distributions depending on jurisdiction and account type. It can also increase exposure to the same issuer without a fresh purchase decision. An investor who already has a concentrated position may prefer to receive cash and allocate it elsewhere. Another may value automation and fractional purchases. Compare those approaches against transaction costs, diversification and cash needs rather than assuming reinvestment is always superior.

sections.heading: Read results as scenarios, not targets
sections.text: A scenario with an unchanged payout is optimistic if cash generation is deteriorating. A dividend cut reduces the cash available for future purchases, and a permanent decline in asset value can overwhelm years of reinvestment. Separate your contributions from modeled investment income when reviewing a final balance. A larger balance funded mostly by additional savings is not evidence of extraordinary performance. Vary one assumption at a time so the source of a change remains understandable.

example.heading: Hypothetical: the first monthly step
example.text: Start with $10,000 at a constant 6% annual yield and assume no withholding. The first monthly distribution in this simplified model is $10,000 × 6% ÷ 12 = $50. Reinvesting it creates a $10,050 balance before any end-of-month contribution. This is a modeling convention, not an actual monthly payment schedule or price forecast.

pitfall: A smooth rising chart reflects smooth assumptions. It does not demonstrate that the investment is safe or that income will remain constant.
checklist: Check the broker or issuer's reinvestment terms and fees.
State whether yield, dividend per share or share price is held constant.
Separate contributions from reinvested income.
Consider concentration, taxes and the possibility of a dividend cut.

title: REITs and interest rates: more than one transmission channel
description: Separate financing costs, property valuation, tenant demand and rent growth when thinking about interest-rate changes.

sections.heading: Debt costs move on a schedule
sections.text: A change in market interest rates does not instantly reprice every dollar of a REIT's debt. Fixed-rate borrowings remain at their contractual rates until refinancing or another relevant event. Floating-rate debt may respond sooner, subject to the benchmark, spread, floors and hedging. Read the debt maturity schedule and derivative notes together. A low average coupon can describe the existing book while concealing a much higher rate on the next borrowing.

sections.heading: Property values depend on required returns
sections.text: Investors may demand higher yields from property when alternative yields rise, but the relationship is not mechanical. Property cap rates also reflect growth expectations, risk, transaction evidence and asset quality. In a simplified constant-NOI calculation, a higher cap rate lowers value. Real property income can change at the same time. Applying a single cap rate to a diverse portfolio can therefore obscure more than it explains.

sections.heading: The operating backdrop can pull the other way
sections.text: Higher rates may accompany stronger nominal growth and opportunities to raise rents. Short leases can reset faster but also expose landlords to weaker demand more quickly. Long leases can stabilize contractual revenue while fixed escalators lag inflation. If rate cuts arrive during a recession, cheaper financing may be offset by tenant stress and vacancies. The direction of rates alone is not an investment thesis.

sections.heading: Use a bridge from rate change to per-share outcome
sections.text: Start with the amount of debt actually repricing, multiply by the change in effective rate, and translate the incremental interest into an approximate per-share effect. Then examine rental growth, asset sales, hedges and equity issuance separately. This avoids assuming that a favorable funding change benefits each share equally. New shares can spread the benefit more widely, and accounting classifications may differ from cash payments. Check management's guidance assumptions and the maturity note before extending a simple sensitivity into a forecast.

example.heading: Hypothetical: a refinancing step-up
example.text: If $200 million of debt moves from 3% to 5%, annual interest rises by $4 million before fees, hedges or changes in principal. With 100 million common shares, that is $0.04 per share of additional annual interest. It is an isolated sensitivity; operations, taxes and the issuer's adjusted measures may produce a different overall result.

pitfall: REITs do not uniformly rise when rates fall or fall when rates rise. Debt structure, growth expectations and the reason rates changed matter.
checklist: Separate fixed, floating and hedged debt.
Identify maturities rather than applying the new rate to all debt.
Stress cap rates and NOI independently.
Translate financing changes into per-share terms.

title: A REIT research checklist: from business model to open questions
description: A repeatable, evidence-first worksheet for reviewing a REIT without reducing the analysis to a single score.

sections.heading: Map the cash engine
sections.text: Write a short description of the assets, customers and contracts before collecting ratios. Identify the property sectors, geographic exposure and tenant concentration. Note the revenue model: contractual lease payments, short-term rentals, operating revenue or financing spreads. A good description explains who pays, why they keep paying and what would interrupt the payment. If you cannot explain the revenue driver, a precise valuation multiple is premature.

sections.heading: Reconcile the operating result
sections.text: Record revenue, property-level income and the issuer's preferred performance measures with matching periods. For equity REITs, inspect the FFO reconciliation and the full AFFO definition where supplied. Separate total-company growth from per-share growth. Compare cash collection with reported rent and ask what recurring capital spending sits outside an adjusted measure. A checklist should surface uncertainty rather than convert every missing disclosure into an assumed zero.

sections.heading: Place the dividend inside the capital structure
sections.text: Use an appropriate common-share earnings or cash measure and a consistent dividend period. Inspect preferred claims, secured and unsecured debt, maturity concentrations, floating-rate exposure and available liquidity. Consider whether distributions, development and acquisitions compete for the same cash. A comfortable current payout ratio may coexist with a difficult refinancing year. Conversely, a temporarily weak ratio may reflect a transition that deserves further investigation rather than an automatic conclusion.

sections.heading: Write two interpretations and a verification plan
sections.text: State the strongest reasonable explanation for improvement and the strongest plausible reason it could disappoint. For example, contractual escalators may support growth, while lease expirations and tenant incentives could absorb it. List the next disclosures that would distinguish those outcomes: cash rent collection, renewal spreads, capex or the final financing terms. Keep historical facts, your calculations and your inferences separate. This produces a reusable research note rather than a buy-or-sell label that hides its assumptions.

example.heading: Hypothetical: the missing denominator
example.text: A company reports AFFO rising from $100 million to $110 million, while diluted shares rise from 50 million to 60 million. AFFO per share falls from $2.00 to about $1.83 despite 10% total growth. The next question is whether the new capital's earnings contribution is fully reflected in the period, not simply whether total AFFO rose.

pitfall: A checklist is a way to organize evidence. Passing a chosen number of checks is not a probability of safety, a credit rating or an investment recommendation.
checklist: Business: assets, tenants, lease structure and concentrations.
Operations: occupancy, collection, same-store growth and reinvestment.
Measures: reconciliations, periods and diluted shares.
Funding: debt maturities, liquidity, equity and preferred claims.
Conclusion: competing interpretations and unresolved evidence.
